passage:
Kiran: Papa checked my bank statement again. Asked why there were two cafe charges 😔
Salma: Ugh. Is he going to stop your allowance?
Kiran: He said "if you can't explain, I'll hold next month's". I nearly told him it was for books.
Salma: Did you?
Kiran: No. I stopped myself. Lying would only make it worse.
Salma: True. What if you propose a budget? Rent, food, fun, all fixed?
Kiran: And send him a monthly sheet so he doesn't need to check? That could work.
Salma: And the freelance editing idea?
Kiran: Starting it this week. Then the cafe is my own money 😅
Salma: Good plan.

qa.q: What did Papa ask about on the statement?
qa.a: Why there were two cafe charges.

qa.q: Why did Kiran nearly say the charges were for books, and why did Kiran stop?
qa.a: Kiran feared losing next month's allowance, but realised that lying would only make things worse.

qa.q: What plan do Kiran and Salma come up with?
qa.a: A fixed budget for rent, food and fun, a monthly sheet sent to Papa, and freelance editing to earn Kiran's own money.

qa.q: How might Kiran's father see the monthly sheet?
qa.a: He may feel reassured and see less need to check the statement, since his checking probably comes from worry about money.

grounding: Kiran's parents track spending and hold the allowance as leverage; Kiran negotiates a clear budget, shares information and builds own income.

passage:
In their house near the Nashik bus depot, Sudha's father went through her phone payments every Sunday evening. "Forty rupees at the tea stall? Twice?" And when she mentioned the college drama club trip, he said, "Then no pocket money this month."
Her younger brother Chaitanya whispered later, "Just say the book cost more. I do it all the time."
Sudha shook her head. She didn't want to become someone who invented bills.
Instead, on Sunday, she brought a notebook to the veranda. "Baba, what if we fix a monthly amount for me? Bus, lunch, stationery, a little extra. I'll write everything down and show you once a month, not every day." She added, "And I've started teaching two Class 8 kids on Saturdays, so I'll pay for the trip myself."
Her father frowned at the notebook, then at her. "You wrote all this?"
"Yes."
He tapped the page. "Once a month, then. And show me the tuition money too."
"I will."

qa.q: How often did Sudha's father go through her phone payments?
Why did Sudha refuse Chaitanya's idea of inflating the book price?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable with lying and did not want to become someone who invents bills.

qa.q: What did Sudha propose to her father?
qa.a: A fixed monthly amount, written records shown once a month, and paying for the trip herself from her Saturday tuition earnings.

qa.q: How does Baba react to Sudha's notebook?
qa.a: He is surprised and frowns, but agrees to monthly checks and asks to see the tuition money too.

grounding: Shows a parent tracking every rupee and using money as leverage, and answering with a clear budget, shared records and one's own income rather than lies.

passage:
Abebe's mother sent the monthly transfer from Addis Ababa on the first, and on the second came the phone call: "Your statement shows 60 dollars at a music shop. Are you studying medicine or guitar? If the grades drop, the money stops."
In their Toronto flat, his roommate Kaito listened to him pace. "You could just tell her it was textbooks," Kaito offered. "She can't check the shop from there."
Abebe had thought of it. He didn't want his parents funding a lie. "Then every call becomes a test I'm cheating on."
He spent that weekend on a spreadsheet: rent, food, transit, books, and a small line called "mine". He applied for weekend shifts at the campus bookstore. Then he called home.
"Mama, I'll send you my budget every month, and my grades each term. The guitar money will come from my job, not from you. But please don't use the transfer to threaten me. I'd rather we talk."
Her voice softened. "Send the budget. And play me something on the guitar."

qa.q: How much did Abebe spend at the music shop?
How did Abebe feel after his mother's call?
qa.a: Controlled and frustrated, pacing the flat, yet unwilling to lie to her.

qa.q: How did Abebe respond instead of lying?
qa.a: He made a clear budget with a line for himself, offered to share it and his grades, and planned to earn his own guitar money from bookstore shifts.

qa.q: How does Abebe's mother react once she hears the plan?
qa.a: Her voice softens; she asks for the budget and to hear him play the guitar.

grounding: Illustrates a parent using funds as leverage, and negotiating a clear budget, sharing information and building one's own income instead of lying.
